Field surveys of the Multispotted lanternfish Scopelopsis multipunctatus in the subtropical convergence zone off southern Australia reveal that the maximum adult body mass attained by this mesopelagic species is 6.71 grams [Wwi = 6.71 grams]. This teleost exhibits a pronounced diel vertical migration pattern, ascending from daytime depths of approximately 600 meters into the upper 100 meters at night to exploit the deep scattering layer's concentrated zooplankton. The species reaches an ultimate standard length of 9.1 centimeters [Li = 9.1 centimeters], placing it among the smaller-bodied myctophids in its genus. Morphometric analyses of preserved specimens indicate that body shape is laterally compressed and moderately robust, typical of active vertical migrators with relatively high aspect-ratio caudal fins. Pigmentation is distinctive, with multiple rows of small photophores along the flanks, a pattern that likely serves in bioluminescent counter-illumination to obscure the fish's silhouette from predators below. Despite its diminutive size, this lanternfish is relatively long-lived compared to other myctophids of similar body dimensions.

The onset of gonadal activity in Scopelopsis multipunctatus occurs once individuals attain a standard length at puberty of 6.2 centimeters [Lp = 6.2 centimeters], corresponding to a wet weight at puberty of 1.93 grams [Wwp = 1.93 grams]. Histological examination of ovarian tissue from mid-trawl collections indicates that vitellogenesis is initiated during the austral spring, with peak spawning activity coinciding with the summer phytoplankton bloom when food availability for larvae is maximized. Males exhibit a slightly faster maturation trajectory, reaching functional spermatogenesis at a marginally smaller body size than females, a pattern frequently observed in myctophids where male reproductive success is less tied to body size. The energetic impetus for this reproductive development is substantial, as the species must divert resources from somatic growth toward the production of gametes, a transition marked by a perceptible decrease in the rate of length increase after puberty. Population-level variation in size at maturity has been documented across the species' range, with individuals from warmer, more oligotrophic waters maturing at a somewhat larger size, though the underlying mechanism remains unclear.

Under the thermal regime characteristic of its mesopelagic habitat, consistently measured at 8.9 °C [T = 8.9 °C], the Multispotted lanternfish exhibits a maximum recorded lifespan of 1,095 days [am = 1,095 days]. This longevity, equivalent to approximately three years, is relatively protracted for a myctophid of this stature and likely reflects the low metabolic costs associated with inhabiting the cold, oxygen-rich waters of the subtropical gyre. Age determination was performed by counting daily increments in sagittal otoliths from a sample of 247 individuals captured during multiple cruises, with the oldest individual confirming this lifespan estimate. Recruitment of young-of-the-year into the adult population occurs predominantly during the late summer months, following a larval pelagic phase of several weeks duration. The species' annual mortality rate is elevated in the first year of life, typical of many small marine teleosts, but stabilizes at a lower level for sexually mature adults, allowing the relatively extended reproductive window that characterizes this lanternfish compared to its shorter-lived congeners.

Reproductive output in this species is constrained by both its small body size and stable thermal environment. Maximum daily egg production was assessed at 8.9 °C [T = 8.9 °C] in laboratory-maintained gravid females, yielding an average of 214 eggs per day [Ri = 214 eggs per day]. This daily reproductive rate, combined with the species' iteroparous spawning strategy, allows for substantial annual fecundity relative to body mass. The eggs are small and pelagic, measuring approximately 0.3 millimeters in diameter, with a corresponding wet weight at birth of 0.000014 grams [Wwb = 0.000014 grams] calculated from the spherical egg volume. This extremely small initial mass reflects the minimal yolk reserves provided to the embryo, necessitating rapid development and an early transition to exogenous feeding. The planktonic larval phase is consequently brief, with yolk-sac larvae first observed in net hauls within three to four days of spawning at the prevailing temperature, highlighting the species' adaptation to energy-rich but ephemeral food patches in the open ocean.

Comparative life-history analysis places Scopelopsis multipunctatus within a conservative continuum of myctophid demographic strategies. Its ultimate standard length of 9.1 centimeters [Li = 9.1 centimeters] is typical of the genus Scopelopsis, which encompasses moderate-sized lanternfishes with a circumglobal distribution in temperate and subtropical waters. The species' asymptotic body mass of 6.71 grams [Wwi = 6.71 grams] aligns with values reported for other members of the Myctophidae that occupy a similar trophic niche, preying primarily on copepods and euphausiids. The size at which puberty occurs, 6.2 centimeters [Lp = 6.2 centimeters] standard length, represents approximately sixty-eight percent of the ultimate length, a proportional value consistent with the onset of reproduction occurring well before growth ceases, a common pattern among iteroparous fishes. This protracted growth after maturity, from 1.93 grams [Wwp = 1.93 grams] at pubertal onset to the ultimate mass, indicates a substantial allocation of resources to increasing body size even as reproductive effort commences.
